The company is to report back when the option ends, around January 2027, and building would need a separate approval.

"In six months, if we don't like it, we can walk away," Commissioner Verlyn Bolinger said. During the option the company will study utilities, review land use and survey the site. Local station KSNF/KODE described a 10-megawatt, 26-acre project on the north end of town, near the Tank Connection offices. Clay Roberts of HyperDatagrid told commissioners the company would be "as upfront and as transparent as we possibly can."

The city is selling the project on water sales. One of the company's cooling plans uses very little water; the other would use up to 50,000 gallons a day as it grows. Utilities Director Derek Clevenger said that amount "would take just about an hour a day to make with our water plant," which runs at about half its capacity even at the summer peak. The city estimates up to $150,000 a year in water sales and up to $150,000 a year in utility franchise fees. "This is exactly what we're looking for," Mayor Kevin Cruse said.

Nodaway County has no zoning, so commissioners say they had little say over the biggest project ever proposed there. Chicago-based ReLoad pitched a data center in December 2025; after New Jersey's Scale Microgrids bought it in February 2026, it became White Cloud Acres, a hyperscale AI data center and a 600-megawatt natural gas plant on more than 500 acres south of Maryville. The county has put the cost at $6.3 billion, and the company has not named an operator or bought the land.

The company's account has shifted. Commissioners first described an off-grid gas plant; by June, Scale said the electric grid would be the data center's main power source, with the plant running two to four hours a day on average. Early estimates of a million gallons of water a day gave way to about 70,000 gallons, mostly for the power plant, drawn from Maryville's treated wastewater. Scale expects construction to start in early 2027 and estimates 100 to 130 jobs.

About 200 people showed up when the group Nodaway Says No organized against the project. "This is not a fight over advancing technology. This is a fight over power and who should and should not have it," said organizer Holly Caviness. On July 21 the county commission unanimously imposed a six-month moratorium, extendable by six months. Presiding Commissioner Bill Walker said he wants the end user named first; Scale's attorney said none has been chosen.

Microsoft plans a data center campus on 128 of the nearly 272 acres of farmland it bought in 2024 off 144th Avenue near U.S. 131 in Dorr Township, paying more than $48 million. The land is already zoned to allow a data center, so the township cannot simply refuse it; instead the Township Board passed a 12-month moratorium in late February 2026, running to about February 2027, to give the Planning Commission time to write new rules. Microsoft has not disclosed the campus's power use, water use or schedule.

Neighbors worry about water, noise and lost farmland. "We are a rural community," Linda Dumond told WWMT at a January protest. At a residents' meeting later that month, Chris Potter said, "They want our Great Lakes. They want our water." The board chose 12 months over the six its attorney suggested, with Treasurer Sheila Reitz, Clerk Debbie Sewers and Trustees Pat Champion and Dan Weber in favor. Speaking for Microsoft, Jonah Miller said the company supported the township taking its time: "We will pay our own way."

The Village of Lake Isabella is writing data center rules before any developer has come. Its draft Ordinance 2026-04 would bar large-scale and hyperscale data centers everywhere in the village and allow small-scale ones only as a special land use in the Industrial District, according to the village's planning commission minutes for July 14, 2026. Staff said the intent was to regulate data centers rather than encourage them, and that regulation would give the village more legal protection under the Michigan Zoning Enabling Act than an outright ban. Asked whether any developer had approached the village, staff said no inquiries had been received. The only land now zoned Industrial is village-owned property around the Department of Public Works.

Residents asked for more. At the Aug. 11 planning commission meeting, speakers raised low-frequency noise, emergency response to battery fires, the size threshold for a "small-scale" facility and the future of the Cal Brewer Memorial Airport property, and one asked for a 365-day moratorium. The commission voted 6-0 to recommend the ordinance, and members urged residents to stay involved with Isabella County and surrounding townships, since development outside the village could still affect it. On Aug. 18 the Village Council voted 6-0 for a temporary moratorium on data centers through its Nov. 17, 2026 meeting while it reviews the ordinance, the council minutes record.

No data center project in Isabella County has been reported. The one site this map places here, labelled Google Detroit Edge, carries only the address 'Michigan, United States' and is pinned near the geographic centre of the state, which falls in Isabella County; it does not appear to be a project in the county.
No county-level data center rules or proposals were found in published reports, and no news coverage of the village's action was found; this account rests on the village's own minutes.
/data-centers/united-states/michigan/isa.unconfirmed: The minutes are PDFs read with a text extractor. AI-generated summaries of the same meetings on Citizen Portal were not used. This site's 'Google Detroit Edge' entry, with a 1,000MW capacity and a source URL about Council Bluffs, Iowa, appears to be a mis-geocoded or mislabelled record.

paragraphs: Kearney has hosted data centers for more than a decade and just wrote new rules for them. A cryptocurrency mine run by Marathon Digital Holdings opened at Tech oNE Crossing, east of town, in 2017. On Sept. 8, 2026, the Kearney City Council approved a conditional use permit for Project Horizon, a data center by Starwood Digital Ventures (SDV) and MARA that would replace the mine and reuse its 100 megawatts of power for a first phase, reaching 368 megawatts at full buildout.

The developers promised money to the city: $250,000 each over five years to Central Community College and Kearney Public Schools, $250,000 to Hot Meals USA, and 59 permanent jobs. City Manager Brenda Jensen said electricity revenue to the city could rise from about $2 million a year to $11 million to $13 million, and the project's first phase alone would generate about $20 million a year in property taxes for the county and schools. Construction could start by December 2026, with operations by March 2028; the site would have 54 backup generators.

The city's new rules came from an earlier fight. In May 2026, resident Josh Lillyman's petition over noise from a smaller planned site, Sequitor Edge, passed 450 signatures. An advisory group of residents, officials and council members then wrote about 10 pages of data center rules, including a 55-decibel noise limit at the property line and required water studies. "This will be the most regulated industry in Kearney," Jensen said.

Socorro County has no zoning, so when a developer proposed the largest data center in New Mexico on land outside town, residents went to every public body that would listen. In March 2026 Jason Bak, chief executive of Green Data, told the Socorro Electric Cooperative board he wanted to build a 2-gigawatt data center powered by a 10-gigawatt solar farm on 10,000 acres west of Socorro Peak and north of Highway 60, on land owned by New Mexico Tech, El Defensor Chieftain and DCD reported. A public records request later showed the university had signed a non-binding letter of intent on Jan. 5 for a 99-year ground lease of roughly 16 square miles with Aetherion Inc., on whose behalf Bak signed; it also mentioned 200 megawatts of small modular nuclear reactors, which Bak said had since been dropped. Bak said the project would draw water from the air through atmospheric water generation rather than from aquifers, Source NM reported.

Residents doubted it. "There's just nothing concrete that this man has done," Val Thomas, who runs the Facebook page Concerned Socorro, told KRWG. Source NM reported that Bak and Green Data had never built a data center and that several of his earlier ventures, including a solar-powered crypto mine proposed in southern Illinois, never got off the ground. About 100 people attended a May 15 New Mexico Tech Regents meeting and more than 200 a town hall on May 19; Sergio Garza, a data analyst at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, told the regents the heat load would equal "about three Hiroshima bombs a day." The Village of Magdalena passed a resolution opposing the project on May 11, a petition gathered more than 4,600 signatures, and U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez urged the county to act.

On June 2 New Mexico Tech President Michael Jackson said the university would not proceed, citing the lack of contiguous land, the difficulty of due diligence on so large a project, community concerns and the lack of data from a comparable facility, though he left the door open to a revised proposal. On June 9 the Socorro County Commission unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on data centers and related infrastructure on unincorporated land and began forming a Blue Ribbon Committee to recommend regulations; County Manager Joe Chavez chose 15 members from 35 applicants. "We really appreciate you guys. You listened to us, you acted," resident Jon Hertz told the commission. Bak spoke during public comment, saying the data center would generate $50 million a year in local economic impact at full operation and that "we're not other projects all across the country."
The moratorium runs to June 2027. What the committee will recommend, and whether Green Data will return with a smaller proposal, is not known.
/data-centers/united-states/new-mexico/s.unconfirmed: The vote is dated June 9 by El Defensor Chieftain and 'Tuesday evening' in Source NM's June 10 story. Bak's economic-impact and water claims are his own. The Illinois project was reported by El Defensor Chieftain, via KRWG, as a solar array in Murphysboro under a different company, Solar Alliance; Source NM describes a solar-powered crypto mine in southern Illinois; the two may be the same project. The June 2027 end date is inferred from the one-year term.

paragraphs: The former Remington Arms factory in Ilion made guns for more than 200 years before it closed in 2024. Its new owner, Turin Hoefler Avenue LLC, has told the state it wants to turn part of the plant into a data center: a 250,000-square-foot building on Site C, a second the same size later on Site E, and 200 megawatts of power costing $2 billion to $3 billion, Data Center Dynamics reported. Soil there is contaminated with arsenic and mercury above state standards and would need cleanup first, CNY Central reported.

Residents organized before any permit was filed. Close to 100 people marched in Ilion on June 17, 2026. "If you wait until there's a permit or something, guess what? It's too late," said organizer Jax Sweeney, a former Remington union employee, who said she supported redeveloping the plant but not as a data center. "We're not against Turin," she said. "We just want viable businesses for Ilion." David Murray, elected mayor the day before in a write-in campaign, said opposition to a data center was one of his platforms: "We don't want a data center in the Village of Ilion."

Critics point to the village's water system. Mike Cecconi of Little Falls, whose father worked at Remington, told Mohawk Valley Today that Ilion's "fragile, crumbling, underfunded water infrastructure" made it the worst place for such a project. The state legislature passed a one-year moratorium on permitting and construction of new large-scale data centers on June 5, and Governor Kathy Hochul separately ordered a one-year pause on new hyperscale data centers while the state writes standards.
Turin and its environmental consultant did not respond to Mohawk Valley Today's requests for comment. No permit application has been filed for the site, and officials say the plans remain fluid.

Stokes County has now approved the same data center twice. Project Delta, proposed by Charlotte-based Engineered Land Solutions (ELS) on land owned by Triad developer David Couch's DFC Stokes companies, would put a campus of up to 5 million square feet on about 1,000 of nearly 1,845 acres of farmland off Highway 311 near Walnut Cove, close to Duke Energy's coal-fired Belews Creek Power Station. On January 12, 2026, county commissioners voted 3-2 to rezone the land to heavy manufacturing and add data centers as a permitted use countywide, despite a planning board recommendation against it and nearly 30 public speakers opposed.

In March, the Southern Coalition for Social Justice and the Southern Environmental Law Center sued on behalf of residents, arguing the hearings had not been properly noticed. The commissioners then voided both decisions, saying they had made "our own errors in the process," and rejected calls for a moratorium. ELS filed a new rezoning application in July, and on September 14 the board again voted 3-2 to approve it after more than three hours of comment; residents who spoke immediately before the vote were uniformly opposed.

ELS chief executive Drew Nations has estimated $20 million a year in property tax at half buildout and $40 million at full buildout, and says the campus will use closed-loop cooling and draw no water from the Dan River. The end user has not been named, and the power demand, reported only as several hundred megawatts, has not been confirmed by the developer. Nations has said construction could begin within 18 months of the September approval and take three to five years.

A rezoning that Vance County approved in April without the word "data center" in it has turned into a 900-megawatt proposal, enough power for several hundred thousand homes. In April 2026 the county commissioners voted 6-1 to rezone a 40-acre parcel on U.S. 158 Business near Henderson, between Pine Meadow Trail and Horseshoe Bend Road, from Employment and Institutional to Light Industrial for Natelli Investments, a Maryland company that had just withdrawn a 250-megawatt data center plan in Apex after opposition, DCD and WRAL reported. Natelli did not confirm the land was for a data center. "You just sold out," one woman shouted at the board; the commission declined to say who had cast the lone vote against.

Residents pressed for a pause. Ahead of a listening session hosted by Gov. Josh Stein's office, they raised energy bills, water use and noise, noting the site's proximity to homes, a school and an animal shelter. "We're not anti-progress in Vance County," one resident told WRAL. "We want our voices to be heard, but we have felt that they have been completely ignored." Petitions against the project and for a one-year moratorium gathered hundreds of signatures.

In September, as the county discussed a moratorium and new data center rules, Natelli Holdings filed a development plan. In a Sept. 9 letter signed by Tom Natelli, the company said the uncertainty was "very problematic for us at this stage of our efforts. We therefore reluctantly made the decision today to file a plan for development of the site," and attached a marked-up copy of the county's draft ordinance with its preferred changes on setbacks, buffers, cooling and decommissioning, WIZS reported. The Henderson Dispatch described the project as a four-million-square-foot, 900-megawatt campus off U.S. 158 and Poplar Creek Road, in what was once Triangle North Vance. Because Natelli filed first, it has secured "permit choice" under state law, allowing it to choose which rules to follow, the Dispatch reported.

On Sept. 14, 2026 the commissioners adopted a 60-day moratorium on new data center proposals, which many speakers said was too short; it runs through Nov. 13, 2026, when the board can extend it or let new rules take effect. Natelli has said it has been talking with Duke Energy about power and will hold community meetings at an appropriate time. Its end user, water use and schedule have not been disclosed.

Applied Digital is finishing Polaris Forge 2, a $3 billion, 280-megawatt AI data center on farmland east of Interstate 29 between Fargo and Harwood. About 1,800 workers are completing two 907,000-square-foot buildings, and the company says part of the campus will open by the end of 2026 and the rest in early 2027. The Harwood City Council approved the rezoning on September 10, 2025, which let the Texas company break ground.

The approval came after two angry meetings. At the first vote on September 2, residents shouted at Mayor Blake Hankey and one person was removed; Hankey said he hoped the project would "stop Fargo from coming into our backyard." The final vote came without discussion or public comment, with Hankey joining by video from Portugal. "They're acting like good little lap dogs right now," resident Michael Swartz said of the council.

Fargo had tried to annex about 300 acres including the site, and Mayor Tim Mahoney said the city wanted a say over roads, water, power and emergency calls. He also said the center would use 20% of the electricity produced in North Dakota. The Fargo City Commission voted unanimously on December 8, 2025, to drop the annexation.

Power comes from Cass County Electric Cooperative, whose chief executive said the data center will about double the co-op's peak demand but will not drive up rates for existing customers. Applied Digital says it is paying $112 million for a substation and power lines and is getting no tax breaks. It expects 200 to 250 people to work at the site once it opens.

Google is building a $500 million data center, known as Project BOSC, on 373 acres of former farmland off North Cole Street and Bluelick Road in American Township, about seven miles northwest of Lima. Construction is underway, and the county's economic development group says it should be finished by 2030. Google has not said how much power it will use.

The project was arranged in secret. Bistrozzi LLC, a company later revealed as a front for Google, bought the land in 2025, and county commissioners signed a three-year nondisclosure agreement on May 27, 2025. The county cut the data center's property taxes by 75%, with $250,000 a year for 15 years going to Elida Local Schools, and Lima agreed in September 2025 to sell it 5 million to 10 million gallons of water a day for 20 years. Google was named only in March 2026.

Of 325 written comments to the Ohio EPA on the site's 115 backup generators, two supported the project. "This was all done in a very secretive manner, with no public input," said Randy Tooker, who lives half a mile away in Elida. The EPA granted the air permit in late May 2026, allowing the generators to run up to 500 hours a year.

Construction has already reached neighbors. Charlene McCoy, who lives directly east of the site, was hospitalized in April after weeks of construction dust, and the Ohio EPA said it asked the company to contain it. Google sent residents a flier about wells losing pressure or water: "We sincerely apologize for any disruption or concern this may be causing you and your family." The Allen County Port Authority has delayed planned roundabouts "to allow for adjustments in response to public input."

New York developer Thor Equities wants to build the Urbana Technology Hub, a 460,000-square-foot data center near Ohio 55 and U.S. 68 by the Rittal plant in Urbana. The city blocked it and Thor is suing. The project is on hold while the case is in Champaign County Common Pleas Court, where the city's written response is due October 2, 2026.

Urbana first welcomed the project. In April 2025 the city council annexed Thor's land, zoned it for manufacturing and made data centers a permitted use there, and in November 2025 it approved a tax break. After residents learned of the plan in early 2026, the zoning appeals board rejected Thor's site plan, the council passed a 12-month pause on data centers in March, and on June 16 it repealed the rule that allowed them.

Thor also filed a federal lawsuit, saying it spent more than $19 million on the project and that it would bring the city $3 million a year in taxes. Its statement rejected "the misinformation and outright nonsense being spread online about data centers." Outside Urbana, most of Champaign County's townships write their own zoning, and many have moved to ban data centers: the regional planning commission for Logan, Union and Champaign counties reviewed 28 nearly identical township bans between April and September 2026.

Amazon Web Services wants to build a $4 billion data center campus on the 471-acre Cosler Farm along South U.S. 68 in Wilmington, backing onto the Timber Glen subdivision, where some homes are a couple hundred feet away. The city council approved the rezoning and data center rules again in September 2026, but the site plan still needs the planning commission's approval, and a resident's lawsuit over how the council passed the rules is pending before a visiting judge.

Amazon has promised $25 million in water, sewer and road work, including a 1 million-gallon water tower, and 100 permanent jobs with an $8 million payroll. Neighbors worry about noise, generators, air pollution and power bills. Several homeowners sued in federal court, and a judge found the city had broken open meeting rules and ordered the votes redone. The council then passed the rules as emergency measures, which under Ohio law cannot be challenged by referendum. Resident Rachel Brooks sued, saying "the goal of the City seems to be to prevent us from gathering signatures."

Voters will not get a say this November. The Ohio Supreme Court ruled that a citizen initiative setting data center limits on noise, lighting and water could stay off the November 3 ballot because it would let residents sue data centers, which the city has no power to allow. In February 2026 the council also voted 5-2 to rezone about 500 more acres in Wilmington for a second data center by Ardent Technologies. "We're fighting our own representatives," said resident Laura Struve.

Amazon Web Services is planning a data center campus on about 590 acres in Jefferson Township near Jeffersonville, bounded by Interstate 71, State Route 729 and Milledgeville-Jeffersonville Road, next to the Honda and LG battery plant at the Midwest Mega Commerce Center. Amazon paid just over $102 million for the land in 2025 and has committed $5 billion to the county through 2030. A 2024 federal energy filing said the first phase could start operating in September 2026.

Power costs drew the first objection. The Ohio Consumers' Counsel told federal regulators that new transmission for the first phase would cost more than $22 million and that the utility, AES Ohio, planned to seek to spread those costs across its customers. "Amazon pays transmission costs at rates established by utility regulators to make sure we are paying our fair share of the costs for electricity," Amazon spokesperson Virginia Milazzo said.

Land around the site is being annexed into Jeffersonville. In August 2026 the county commissioners accepted petitions to annex 61 more acres along State Route 729 near I-71, filings that listed Amazon Data Services as a neighbor, weeks after 490 acres were annexed. Jefferson Township asked the commissioners to refuse annexations without a joint economic development agreement, and Paint Township resident Dan Drake asked for a pause on data centers there while a land use plan is written.

The only data center idea in Jefferson County so far is for the site of a coal plant being torn down. The W.H. Sammis plant in Stratton on the Ohio River was bought in 2023 by Energy Transition and Environmental Management (ETEM) of Houston, which is demolishing it. In June 2025 ETEM co-founder and general counsel Dan McDevitt asked the county commissioners to have the site designated a priority investment area under Ohio's House Bill 15, which brings faster permit reviews, brownfield funding and a utility tax exemption, the Herald-Star reported.

McDevitt said the site has an on-site switching station and substation, water and rail access, and that ETEM, which sells cleaned-up sites to others, now saw it suiting a data center of around 500 megawatts, possibly fed by a new gas pipeline and gas-fired generation. "We're not data center developers," he said. He estimated billions of dollars in investment, perhaps 1,000 construction jobs and "a couple hundred" permanent jobs. The commissioners were receptive. "Our board will do anything possible to bring in new opportunities to our county," Commissioner Tony Morelli said. Commissioner Jake Kleineke said he would prefer power generation to "a server farm," which he said would strain the local grid.

In September 2026 the commissioners said an unnamed group had asked whether they would discuss a data center at the Sammis site, but that nothing had moved beyond that contact. "There are positives, but there are also some negatives. You know, we don't know about the water sources," Commissioner Eric Timmons told WTOV. "So we want to get educated." No lease, sale or formal application has followed the September inquiry.

Hannibal, on the Ohio River, has been promised a data center before. In 2019 DP Facilities announced plans for one on the site of the former Ormet aluminum smelter, next to the new Long Ridge Energy Terminal gas plant; Monroe County's economic development director, Jason Hamman, said it never came to fruition, the Athens County Independent reported.

Now Mara Holdings, one of the largest bitcoin miners, has agreed to buy the Long Ridge plant and its roughly 1,600-acre site for about $1.5 billion, including $785 million of debt, and says it will start building an initial 200 megawatts of AI data center capacity in the first half of 2027, ready in mid-2028, with room to grow to 600 megawatts through grid expansion and more on-site generation, DCD reported. Mara says it does not intend to reduce the plant's supply to the PJM grid, so consumers should see no direct impact. "Power is the scarce input in AI," chief executive Fred Thiel said.

Hamman is more cautious. Mara had leased a bitcoin mining facility in the area for several years, and he said he believes that facility is what the company now describes as a 200-megawatt data center; he had no job estimates, the Independent reported in August 2026. The gas plant employs about 20 people, whom Mara has said it will keep. The sale was expected to close in the second half of 2026. Monroe County has not adopted a moratorium or other rules for data centers.

Pike County is the proposed home of what federal officials call the largest data center ever planned. On March 20, 2026, cabinet members broke ground on the PORTS Technology Campus at the former Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant south of Piketon, a Cold War uranium enrichment site still being decontaminated. SB Energy, a SoftBank company, plans a campus that could reach 10 gigawatts (10,000 megawatts) of power, starting with an 800-megawatt first phase, powered by a $33 billion, 9.2-gigawatt natural gas plant paid for with Japanese government funds under the U.S.-Japan trade deal, and a $4.2 billion transmission program with AEP Ohio, DCD, WOUB and cleveland.com reported. SoftBank has said the campus would take 35,000 construction workers at peak and about 2,500 to run. OpenAI is in advanced talks to lease the campus, and Nvidia has confirmed it will back about 4.25 gigawatts of it, DCD reported. The March ceremony did not start the build: in August a SoftBank spokesperson, Ally Copple, said the first phase of construction would begin later in 2026, with work on the whole campus continuing through 2032, The Post in Athens reported.

Officials have promised residents their bills will not rise. "I will commit right here, right now, that we will protect the electricity bill," SoftBank chief executive Masayoshi Son said, adding that the company would donate $40 million to the community. County officials' concern is revenue: the federal government still owns most of the 3,700-acre site, so leased land would pay no property tax. "What we're asking is … let's negotiate like it's private property," Commissioner Tony Montgomery told WOUB, saying SB Energy had been open to a payment in lieu of taxes.

Unlike most data center fights, there has been little organized opposition. At an SB Energy open house in Waverly in July, more than 100 residents looked at plans for the gas plant, which would cover 770 acres just south of the enrichment site; Inside Climate News found no sign of an opposition campaign. Gina Doyle, who lives about three miles away and opposes the project, attributed that to the region's long dependence on federal jobs at the plant. Others point to the site's history: Vina Colley, a former PORTS electrician who leads Portsmouth/Piketon Residents for Environmental Safety and Security, told The Post that contamination must be cleaned up before construction, and a 2022 study by epidemiologist Joseph Mangano found Pike County had the highest cancer incidence in Ohio. SoftBank says SB Energy has committed to paying for accelerated cleanup.

The gas plant still needs approval from the Ohio Power Siting Board, the state agency that signs off on power plants, and new pipelines to reach it may take years, the Ohio Oil and Gas Association told cleveland.com.

Preble County's only data center proposal has been withdrawn, but its backers say it will be back. In 2025 PRSM, an Arlington, Virginia, land development company, sought through the landowners to rezone about 298 acres of farmland in Jefferson Township, along Orphans Road south of Interstate 70 near Eaton, so that 270 acres could host a computer data storage center, DCD and The Register-Herald reported. There was no end user lined up. "If we can't find the right buyer, we'll rezone to agriculture," PRSM president Patrick Scanlon told WDTN.

The county's advisory boards turned it down: the Preble County Planning Commission voted 11-0 against on Aug. 21, 2025, and the Rural Zoning Commission 5-0 on Sept. 2, after a hearing that drew an overflow crowd worried about water and electricity bills. On Sept. 29, before the county commissioners could vote, the landowners withdrew the application, saying the process "requires a different approach and will be re-evaluated sometime in the future." Residents had begun organizing a referendum campaign, Signal Ohio reported. "I've never seen the citizens of this county so universally upset and perturbed about something as I have this particular issue," said Gene Krebs, a former Republican state lawmaker from the county.

"Interest in having a data center on that land has not gone away," Scanlon said after the withdrawal. Brad Kramer, the county's land use director, told commissioners that a new application would start over at the planning commission, and that PRSM does not have to wait a year to refile.

Sidney signed a non-disclosure agreement with Amazon on Dec. 19, 2023, and the city had been discussing "Project Galaxy" for more than two years by the time its agreements were final, the Sidney Daily News reported. The $3 billion Amazon Data Services campus is going up north of Millcreek Road and west of Vandemark Road. In October 2025 the city council granted a 30-year, 100% property tax abatement in exchange for $50 million in payments in lieu of taxes over 15 years, DCD reported, citing the Sidney Daily News and WHIO.

In April 2026 the council unanimously approved the remaining agreements before a room packed beyond capacity. Under the 10-year water deal, the campus may draw up to 1 million gallons a day from the city system, which has 3.9 million gallons a day of spare treatment capacity, but its projected use is about 12,600 gallons a day. Amazon will contribute up to $8 million to rebuild Millcreek Road, the Sidney Daily News reported.

Residents asked the council to wait. Kristin Allen, who founded Sidney Citizens for Responsible Development, cited her pending public records dispute in the Ohio Court of Claims over redactions in the agreements. "There's a lot of people that live in that area," resident Tim Fisher told the council, "and I could guarantee each and every one of you on the council, if you had family members that lived out there, you would not want this business that close to your family." Asked about the power source and backup generation, City Manager Jon Crusey said that was between Amazon and AES.

Mayor Mike Barhorst defended the process. "I'm satisfied that this council, ably aided by our staff, has done our due diligence," he said, and criticized "false accusations" against council members from some opponents, including people who did not live in the city. The site plan is now with city staff, not the council. Construction moved forward through the summer of 2026, and city officials project about 75 permanent jobs by late 2030, Construction Review Online reported.

Amazon's plans for Floyd County surfaced through state filings. Amazon Data Services has filed with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation to build three data center buildings, together called Horizon Junction, at 1782 and 1774 County Road 241 in Floydada, each 189,060 square feet and $300 million, with construction running from August 2026 to April 2027, Data Center Dynamics reported. The site currently holds the nine-hole Floydada County Club golf course; DCD found no public announcement that the club is closing.

The county has little power to shape it. Floyd County commissioners say their limited authority leaves them few tools over what could grow to seven buildings on about 485 acres worth more than $1 billion, RFD News reported in August 2026. They are weighing a Chapter 312 tax abatement that would require air-cooled systems, to limit groundwater use, and require the project to generate its own power so it does not compete with homes, farms and businesses during shortages.

Uruguay's largest data center is being built by Google in the Parque de las Ciencias free trade zone at Colonia Nicolich, Canelones, next to homes, schools and sports clubs. Construction began in August 2024 on a US$850 million plan of four stages over 26 months, which would put completion around October 2026. Google has said it will use at most 560 gigawatt-hours of electricity a year, about 5% of national demand, and has a contract with the state utility UTE for 430.

Water forced a redesign. During the severe drought of 2023, the original plan to use up to 7.6 million liters of drinking water a day for cooling became contested; Google shrank the project and switched to air cooling, and the Environment Ministry approved the revised plan. An investigation by Amenaza Roboto, published by the Pulitzer Center, found that if all 27 diesel backup generators ran at once, nitrogen dioxide could reach about 17 times the legal limit, and that the most exposed neighbor, 280 meters away, could face 72 decibels at night during an outage.

The ministry required noise monitoring, a detailed emergency plan and final generator specifications to be settled during construction and operation. Building employs 300 to 400 people, with a peak of about 800, and about 50 will work there once it opens.

The Northern Territory's working data centers are small, but the government says a dozen investors want to build bigger ones. NEXTDC opened D1 Darwin in 2024 and has topped out D2 Darwin, which will add 6 megawatts of power. In mid-2026, Business Minister Robyn Cahill said the government was in talks with 12 investors about proposed data centers, calling the Territory "Australia's digital gateway to Asia" because of its subsea cable links to Southeast Asia.

Two large projects are public. Perth-based Energy North has proposed Project Ares, a 1-gigawatt, off-grid campus on Murranji Station in the Barkly Region, powered by gas and solar and drawing up to 4 gigaliters of water a year, more than greater Darwin uses in a month. In July, the government gave Beetaloo Digital exclusive rights over land at Weddell, 30 kilometers south of Darwin, for a possible 2-gigawatt, gas-powered data center that would use more than six times the region's current peak power demand. "We believe in the next three to four years we could see this project move into production," said managing director Alex Underwood.

Opponents want a pause. "There is zero community consent for these projects," said Pauline Cass of the Environment Centre NT, which along with Greenpeace has called for a moratorium. Neither project has approval or financing, and Beetaloo Energy has not said how it would get its water.

Google bought land for a data center in Kronstorf, Upper Austria, in 2008 and broke ground there on April 23, 2026. The company's first self-built Austrian data center will cover 42,000 square metres, 29,000 of them data center space, on a 70-hectare site near the Enns river, with off-site heat recovery, a green roof with solar panels and about 100 direct jobs, DCD and PPC Land reported. Google has not given an investment figure. Upper Austria's governor, Thomas Stelzer, called it "a powerful signal for Upper Austria as a hub for business and innovation." Google also pledged a fund with the Upper Austrian Fisheries Association to improve the Enns's ecosystem as part of a promise to replenish more freshwater than the site consumes by 2030.

Most of the rest of Austria's capacity is around Vienna. The city has about 82 megawatts of operating capacity, more than 80% of the national total of about 100 megawatts, with about 170 megawatts more in the development pipeline, according to a Colliers report summarised in German by Immobilien-Redaktion, which named power and grid connection times as the main limits. Microsoft says its Austrian cloud region, launched in 2025, is being built at Schwechat, Achau and Vösendorf, south-east of Vienna, but has not said how far construction has progressed or how much power it uses, the public broadcaster ORF reported in German.

The grid operator is being asked for far more. Gerhard Christiner of Austrian Power Grid told ORF, in German, that requests for about 2,500 megawatts of data center capacity had reached his company, with similar volumes at the distribution operators, though not all would be built. The US company CloudHQ plans a campus of up to about 200 megawatts at Leopoldsdorf, just south of Vienna, with construction from 2027, and the Greens in neighbouring Maria Lanzendorf have criticised the lack of studies on noise and heat, ORF reported. ORF also reported, in German, that resistance at Kronstorf had been greater than at Leopoldsdorf.

Regulators are adding conditions. Since July 2026, Vienna has required data centers with more than 1 megawatt of energy input to carry out a cost-benefit analysis of waste heat use before being built or significantly modernised, under the city's 2026 energy law amendments, according to a German-language legal summary by E+H Rechtsanwälte. Lower Austria introduced its own siting rules for data centers in June, ORF reported.
/data-centers/austria/.unconfirmed: German-language sources (ORF, Immobilien-Redaktion, E+H, DataCenter-Insider) are given as reported speech. ORF gives the Kronstorf capacity range as 150 to 500 megawatts; a search summary gave 150MW; Google has not confirmed a figure. The nature of the Kronstorf opposition was not described in the articles opened. PPC Land reports that Google sold 20 of the original 70 hectares in 2018. The Colliers figures are that firm's estimates. A smaller 6.4MW colocation site by Greencore at Kottingbrunn in Lower Austria was reported by DataCenter-Insider but is not described on the page.

paragraphs: Amazon's cloud region in Bahrain was knocked out by war. On March 1, 2026, after joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, a drone strike close to an Amazon Web Services facility in Bahrain caused structural damage, disrupted power and required fire suppression that caused water damage, while two AWS data centers in the United Arab Emirates were hit directly, CNBC reported. Iran's Fars News Agency said the Bahrain facility had been targeted "to identify the role of these centers in supporting the enemy's military and intelligence activities"; Amazon declined to comment on the claim, which CNBC could not verify. A second availability zone was disrupted in April, taking the region fully offline, Help Net Security reported.

On Sept. 15 AWS said it could not recover customer data and resources hosted only in its Bahrain region, me-south-1, which it had announced in 2019 and which hosts significant government workloads. "After a thorough assessment, we have determined that we are unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted exclusively in this region," the company wrote, adding that the damage across multiple availability zones had exceeded what its redundancy was designed to withstand. It said most customers had already moved, and that it would give a further update for Bahrain in early 2027. Fortune reported that the attacks were believed to be the first time data centers had been deliberately targeted for air strikes in a conflict.

Bahrain's local operators are smaller. The telecoms group Beyon commissioned a 6,000-square-metre White Space Data Centre at its Data Oasis campus in southern Bahrain in 2025, which Batelco's chief executive, Maitham Abdulla, called "the largest and most power-dense facility in Bahrain"; it also runs a 2.75-megawatt site at Hamala, supplied in part by its own solar park, DCD reported. Batelco has since leased the new facility to Qareeb Data Centers to operate as an edge data center, w.media reported. Beyon has also agreed with the government's Information & eGovernment Authority to launch an Oracle-based sovereign cloud intended to keep data entirely within Bahrain.
Whether AWS will rebuild in Bahrain, and whether other hyperscale projects will proceed there after the strikes, has not been announced.
/data-centers/bahrain/.unconfirmed: Iran's claims about the purpose of the strike are those of Iranian state media and were not verified. Reports differ on whether the Bahrain site was hit directly: AWS and CNBC describe a nearby strike; some summaries describe a direct hit. The March 1 date is inferred from CNBC's March 4 report that the strike happened on the preceding Sunday. The White Space facility's capacity in megawatts was not given. The 'largest' description is Batelco's.

paragraphs: The newest data center proposal in Flanders is in Lanaken, Limburg. The Dutch company Switch Datacenters is negotiating to build on the former Sappi paper mill site, an investment its spokesperson, Cara Mascini, said could reach €1 billion for the building alone, with 150 to 250 jobs, VRT NWS reported on September 18, 2026. Switch still has to sign with the site's owner and then obtain building permits; it hopes to finish construction five years after signing.

Mayor Marino Keulen welcomed the plan after the closures of the Celanese and Sappi plants. "People should not fear that their own electricity supply will be at risk," he said, adding that Switch plans to reuse its cooling water and he expects no major problems because the site is already industrial. Mascini said the old mill can connect straight to the high-voltage grid rather than the local distribution grid, which she called fairly saturated in Belgium and the Netherlands.

Most of Flanders' existing data centers sit around Brussels, where the Flemish grid operator Fluvius said in 2024 that it sometimes could no longer connect new projects in Flemish Brabant. Digital Realty owns three data centers in Zaventem. De Tijd reported in 2024 that Microsoft was setting up three cloud data centers around Brussels (the trade site Computable named Zaventem, Ternat and Aalst) and that EdgeConnex was building its first Belgian site in Ternat. Elia, the national grid operator, expects data center power use across Belgium to more than double by 2034.

No large data center is being built in Bulgaria yet. The biggest plan is a 3 billion euro AI data center by Brinell Compute, a Munich company, on 809 hectares (about 2,000 acres) of the Rakovski Industrial Zone in Maritsa municipality, north of Plovdiv. Bulgaria's Council of Ministers approved a memorandum of understanding with the company on January 21, 2026, and Brinell says construction will begin this fall.

The project's computing power, customers and financing have not been made public. Brinell was registered in Munich in September 2025 with capital of 25,000 euros, bne IntelliNews reported; the company says it has developed more than 4 gigawatts of energy projects. Local officials told Blitz.bg the Maritsa site would be "a specialized data center with enormous computing power and supercomputers," not a robot factory.

In May, Innovation Minister Tomislav Donchev said the government had authorized three new data center projects: one with the German firm Schwarz Digits, one with another German company and one with a large US developer. The one data center listed below, Equinix's SO1, is in Sofia.

Scala Data Centers, owned by DigitalBridge, plans a huge AI data center campus called Scala AI City on about 700 hectares in Eldorado do Sul, across Lake Guaíba from Porto Alegre. It would start with a R$3 billion, 50-megawatt building and could grow to about 5 gigawatts. On September 3, 2026, the national electricity regulator Aneel authorized it to connect straight to the 525-kilovolt Guaíba transmission line, for demand of up to 1.8 gigawatts by 2033. Its environmental license is pending before the state agency Fepam.

Scala applied to Fepam in May and says building could start in 2027, with the first unit running between late 2028 and early 2029, if its licenses come on time. Ambiental Media reported that a 2024 agreement with the state promised "simplified environmental licensing," which skips a full impact study; the state says there will be no relaxing of legal requirements. State deputy Matheus Gomes, who chairs a legislative panel on data centers, said 1.8 gigawatts is 40% more than all the state's homes use on average: "The licensing needs to be rigorous."

Eldorado do Sul was the town worst hit by the 2024 floods and went weeks without power. Residents told Ambiental the local grid is already unreliable. "The power goes out all the time, on and off several times a day," said Úrsula Silva Pedroso, who lives in the town center, and people in the Guaíba City subdivision, 4 kilometers from the site, blocked a road for 14 days over regular outages. Fepam said it may ask Scala for more information and additional studies.

Ningxia's data centers are concentrated in Zhongwei, a desert city on the southern edge of the Tengger Desert that is one of China's national computing hubs. Its Western Cloud Base now holds nine data center parks, including those of Amazon, China Communications Construction, China Mobile and China Telecom, plus backup data centers for eight central government bodies, Xinhua reported in March 2026. The newest is China Communications Construction's park, recently opened, with more than 140 megawatts of computing load.

Amazon's cloud has been here since 2017, when AWS opened its China (Ningxia) region with two availability zones run by a local partner, Ningxia Western Cloud Data Technology, to meet Chinese law. The data center operator Chindata has announced a 24 billion yuan cluster of three data centers in Zhongwei, which DCD headlined as 1.2 gigawatts, without a timeline or exact site. Xinhua says 13 AI models, including Baidu's and Tencent's, are trained in Zhongwei.

Building the base had a local cost: the city relocated farmers who grew the wolfberries and watermelons Zhongwei is known for to make room for the industrial park, the research institute MERICS reported.
